title: Ellipsis and Substitution
description: Learn how proficient speakers and writers avoid repetition by leaving out recoverable words and by using substitutes such as so, not, do so and one(s), adjusting the choice to register.
objectives: Use ellipsis after auxiliaries, modals and infinitive 'to'
Respond economically with so/neither/nor, short answers, tags and echo questions
Substitute clauses with so and not, including if so and if not
Choose correctly between do so, do it, do too and one/ones
Write concise formal prose using gapping, respectively and related devices

lessons.title: Ellipsis after Auxiliaries and To
lessons.summary: Leave out a repeated verb phrase while keeping the auxiliary, modal or infinitive 'to'.
objectives: Omit a repeated verb phrase after an auxiliary or modal
Use do/does/did when the first clause has no auxiliary
Keep 'to' when omitting an infinitive after verbs such as would like, have, ought and used
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### What is ellipsis?
**Ellipsis** means leaving out words that the listener or reader can recover from the context. It is not laziness: in English, repeating a whole verb phrase usually sounds heavy or even unnatural. Compare:
- *She said she would finish the report, and she finished the report.* (clumsy)
- *She said she would finish the report, and she **did**.* (natural)

### Ellipsis after auxiliaries and modals
The most common type keeps the **auxiliary or modal** and drops everything after it:

| Full form | Elliptical form |
|---|---|
| I haven't read it yet, but I will read it. | I haven't read it yet, but I **will**. |
| He can't come, but his deputy can come. | He can't come, but his deputy **can**. |
| You should have told me. — I know I should have told you. | — I know I **should have**. |
| Is she coming? — She might be coming. | — She **might be**. |

If the first clause has no auxiliary (present simple or past simple), use **do / does / did**: *Lina enjoys opera, and so **does** her brother. She promised to call, and she **did**.*

The auxiliary must match the **verb you are replacing**: ✗ *He can't swim, but his sister does* → *... but his sister **can***. With *be* as a main verb, keep *be*: *She isn't ready, but I **am**.* With perfect and passive forms you may keep one or more auxiliaries: *Has the parcel been sent? — It **has** / It **has been**.*

### Ellipsis after infinitive 'to'
After verbs such as *want, would like, would love, hope, try, need, have, used, ought, mean, plan*, you can drop the verb phrase but must **keep *to***:
- *Are you coming to the gala? — I'd love **to**, but I'm working.*
- *I didn't want to apologise, but I had **to**.*
- *She doesn't sing as much as she used **to**.*

Dropping *to* as well is wrong after *would like, would love, need, have, ought, used*: ✗ *I'd like, but I can't.* In conditional and relative clauses after *want* and *like*, however, the whole infinitive can disappear: *Come with us if you **want**. Take as many as you **like**.*

### Stress and pronunciation
In elliptical clauses the final **auxiliary is stressed** and pronounced in its full form: *I'm not sure she'll come, but I hope she **will** /wɪl/.* A contraction cannot end the clause: ✗ *... but I hope she'll.* ✗ *I don't know if I can, but I'll.*

### Register
Ellipsis is used in all registers. In formal writing it keeps sentences concise; in conversation it is essential for sounding natural. Full repetition can sound robotic, pedantic or even sarcastic: *Did you lock the door? — Yes, I locked the door.*

lessons.title: Elliptical Responses in Conversation
lessons.summary: Respond economically with so/neither/nor, short answers, question tags, echo questions and situational ellipsis, adjusting to register.
objectives: Agree with positive and negative statements using so/neither/nor + auxiliary + subject
Distinguish 'So do I' (addition) from 'So I do' (confirmation)
Recognise situational ellipsis and keep it out of formal writing
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Agreeing and adding: so / neither / nor
To say that the same is true of another person, English uses *so* (positive) or *neither / nor* (negative) + **auxiliary + subject** (inverted):

| Statement | Same for me | Different for me |
|---|---|---|
| I've finished. | So **have I**. | I haven't. |
| I can't swim. | Neither / Nor **can I**. | I can. |
| I loved the film. | So **did I**. | I didn't. |
| I'm not tired. | Neither **am I**. | I am. |
| I'd rather walk. | So **would I**. | I wouldn't. |

The auxiliary must match the statement (have → have, can't → can, past simple → did). Informal alternatives are *Me too* (positive) and *Me neither* (negative); they are fine in conversation but too casual for formal writing. *I did too* and *I haven't either* are neutral.

### 'So do I' versus 'So I do'
*So + auxiliary + subject* (inverted) **adds a new person**: *Lina speaks Thai. — **So does Raka**.* *So + subject + auxiliary* (not inverted) **confirms something surprising about the same subject**: *You're standing on my foot! — **So I am**. Sorry!*

### Short answers and tags
Short answers repeat the auxiliary, not the main verb: *Have you seen the report? — Yes, I **have**. / No, I **haven't**.* (✗ *Yes, I have seen.*) Question tags work the same way: *You'll call me, **won't you**?* Negative words such as *nobody, never, hardly* make the tag positive, and *nobody / somebody / everyone* take *they*: *Nobody called, **did they**?*

### Echo questions
Short echo questions with the auxiliary show interest, surprise or doubt: *I've resigned. — **Have you?** Why?* *She doesn't eat meat. — **Doesn't she?***

### Situational ellipsis in speech
In informal conversation, speakers drop subjects and auxiliaries at the start of a sentence when the context makes them obvious:
- *(That) Sounds good.*
- *(Have you) Seen Raka anywhere?*
- *(I) Told you so.*
- *(Are you) Coming tonight?*

This is natural in speech and text messages but **not appropriate in formal writing**: ✗ *Dear Dr. Okafor, Received your report. Looks excellent.*

### Register summary
| Formal / neutral | Informal |
|---|---|
| So do I. / Neither can I. | Me too. / Me neither. |
| Did you receive the file? | Get the file? |
| That sounds excellent. | Sounds great. |

In debates and meetings, elliptical responses make agreement and disagreement quick and polite: *I don't think the plan is affordable. — **Nor do I**, frankly.*

Me too.

didn't they
was it
didn't it

lessons.title: Substituting Clauses with So and Not
lessons.summary: Replace whole clauses with so and not after verbs such as think, hope and be afraid, and use if so / if not in formal writing.
objectives: Use so/not after think, believe, expect, suppose, hope and be afraid
Choose between 'I don't think so' and the formal 'I think not'
Use 'if so' and 'if not' to write concise formal instructions
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Substituting a whole clause
After certain verbs and expressions, English replaces an entire *that*-clause with **so** (positive) or **not** (negative):

- *Will the ferry run tomorrow? — I **think so**.* (= I think that it will run.)
- *Is the museum open on Mondays? — I'm **afraid not**.* (= I'm afraid that it isn't open.)

### Which verbs?
| Expression | Positive | Negative |
|---|---|---|
| think, believe, expect, suppose, imagine | I think so. | I don't think so. (neutral) / I think not. (formal) |
| hope | I hope so. | I hope not. (✗ I don't hope so) |
| be afraid (= regret) | I'm afraid so. | I'm afraid not. |
| guess (informal) | I guess so. | I guess not. |
| appear, seem | It appears so. / So it seems. | It seems not. / It appears not. |
| say, tell, hear | So I've heard. / He said so. | — |

### Two negative patterns
With *think, believe, expect, suppose, imagine*, the usual negative puts *not* on the main verb: *I **don't think** so.* The form *I think not* exists but sounds formal, emphatic or even dismissive: *Will the minister resign? — **I think not**.* With *hope* and *be afraid*, only the *not* pattern is possible: ✗ *I don't hope so.* ✗ *I'm not afraid so.*

### If so / if not
In formal writing, *if so* and *if not* replace a whole conditional clause:
- *Please indicate whether you require accommodation and, **if so**, for how many nights.*
- *Check whether the form has been signed. **If not**, return it to the sender.*

These are much more concise than *if you do require accommodation* or *if it has not been signed*.

### So at the front
*So* can also be fronted to refer back to information someone else has given: *The lecture has been cancelled. — **So I've heard** / **So I understand**.* The order is so + subject + verb, without inversion.

### What cannot be substituted
*So* is not normally used after *be sure, be certain* or *agree*: ✗ *I'm sure so* (say *I'm sure* or *I'm sure it will*); ✗ *I agree so* (say *I agree*). With *know*, simply say *I know* or *I don't know*. Never use *it* for this function: ✗ *I think it.* ✗ *I hope it.*

### Tone
Short *so / not* replies are economical but can sound cool or noncommittal. Adding a reason softens them: *I don't think so — the forecast is terrible.* In negotiations and meetings, *I'm afraid not* is the standard polite refusal, while *I think not* can sound superior unless used playfully.

lessons.title: Do So, Do It and One(s)
lessons.summary: Substitute verb phrases with do so, do it, do that and do too, and nouns with one and ones, respecting their grammatical restrictions.
objectives: Use do so in formal writing to replace an intentional action
Avoid do so and do it with stative verbs
Use one/ones only for countable nouns and avoid it with uncountables and bare possessives
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Substituting a verb phrase: do so, do it, do that
Besides simple ellipsis (*She said she would, and she **did***), English can replace a verb phrase with a substitute form.

| Form | Register | Example | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **do so** | formal | *Applicants wishing to withdraw must **do so** in writing.* | Replaces an action; common in rules, reports and academic prose |
| **do it** | neutral/informal | *I need to fix the gate — I'll **do it** tomorrow.* | Refers to a specific, deliberate action |
| **do that** | neutral | *Please don't lean on the glass. Don't **do that**.* | Demonstrative, more emphatic or contrastive |
| **do too / do as well** | neutral | *Lina owns a flat, and Raka **does too**.* | Simple addition; works with any verb |

### Restrictions on do so and do it
*Do so* and *do it* replace **dynamic, intentional actions**. They sound wrong with **stative** verbs such as *know, own, believe, resemble, contain*:
- ✗ *Lina owns a flat in Port Elvan, and Raka **does so** too.*
- ✓ *Lina owns a flat in Port Elvan, and Raka **does** too.*

*Do so* sounds stiff in casual speech; there, use plain ellipsis or *do it*. In formal writing it is very useful, especially with a new subject, time or manner: *The delegates were invited to comment, and several **did so** at length.*

### Substituting a noun: one and ones
*One* (singular) and *ones* (plural) replace a **countable** noun that has already been mentioned, usually after an adjective, *the, this/that, which* or *every*:
- *I prefer the red scarf to the blue **one**.*
- *These boots are too tight. Have you got any bigger **ones**?*
- *Which proposal did they choose? — **The one** from Westmere University.*

### Restrictions on one(s)
1. **Not with uncountable nouns.** ✗ *I prefer white rice to brown one* → *... to brown* / *... to brown rice*. ✗ *She gave me advice, a useful one* → *some useful advice*.
2. **Not directly after a possessive** in careful English: *Your laptop is faster than **mine*** (not *my one*). With an adjective it is fine: *my old one*.
3. **Not 'a one' without an adjective.** ✗ *I need a pen — have you got a one?* → *Have you got **one**?*
4. **Not after a number alone.** ✗ *I ordered three ones* → *I ordered **three***; but *three large ones* is fine.
5. In formal writing, prefer *these* or *those* on their own to *these ones / those ones*.

### Choosing the right substitute
Ask two questions:
1. Is the repeated element a **noun** (→ *one/ones*, or simple ellipsis) or a **verb phrase** (→ auxiliary ellipsis, *do so*, *do it*, *do too*)?
2. Is the verb **dynamic** (any form possible) or **stative** (→ only plain *do/does/did*, often with *too* or *so* + inversion)?

| Repeated element | Formal | Neutral/informal |
|---|---|---|
| intentional action | did so | did it / did |
| state (own, know) | did / so did ... | did too |
| countable noun | the one(s) | the one(s) |
| uncountable noun | ellipsis (*brown*) | ellipsis |

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses 'one' correctly?
questions.instructions: 'One' can only replace a countable noun.
options: Of the two proposals, I prefer the one from the regional office.

She wanted a new bicycle, so she bought a one yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Proposal' is countable, so 'the one from the regional office' is correct. 'Advice' and 'furniture' are uncountable and cannot be replaced by 'one', and 'a one' needs an adjective (a red one).

questions.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically acceptable?
options: Mr. Hartley resembles his grandfather, and his son does too.

Mr. Hartley resembles his grandfather, and his son does it too.
Mr. Hartley resembles his grandfather, and his son so does.

lessons.title: Economy in Formal Writing
lessons.summary: Avoid repetition in formal writing with gapping, conjunction reduction, respectively, likewise, the same and such.
objectives: Use gapping and conjunction reduction with parallel structures
Link ordered lists with 'respectively'
Use likewise, do the same and such to refer back concisely without creating ambiguity
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Economy in formal writing
Formal and academic writing values concision. Instead of repeating verbs, nouns or whole clauses, skilled writers use a set of reduction devices. Each device must leave the meaning completely clear.

### 1. Gapping
In coordinated clauses with parallel structure, the repeated **verb** (and sometimes other material) can be left out of the second clause. A comma often marks the gap:
- *Lina chose economics, and Raka, law.* (= and Raka chose law)
- *Exports fell by 4%; imports, by 2%.*

Gapping works only when the clauses are parallel and the omitted verb is identical in form: ✗ *Lina has chosen economics, and Raka, studying law.*

### 2. Conjunction reduction
When two clauses share a subject or auxiliary, the shared element is stated only once, but the remaining parts must be **grammatically parallel**:
- ✓ *The scheme was welcomed by staff and criticised by unions.* (was + participle, [was] + participle)
- ✗ *The scheme was welcomed by staff and criticising by unions.*

### 3. Respectively
*Respectively* links two lists **in order**, replacing two separate sentences:
- *The first and second sites produced 400 and 250 units **respectively**.*
- *Dr. Amara and Professor Lund were appointed dean and vice-dean, **respectively**.*

The lists must match in number and order, and *respectively* normally comes at the end of the clause. It cannot be used with a single item.

### 4. Likewise, the same and such
| Device | Use | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *likewise* | the same applies to something else | *Staff must wear badges. **Likewise**, visitors must sign in.* |
| *do the same* | repeat an action with a new subject | *The north campus banned cars, and the south campus **did the same**.* |
| *such* + noun | refers back to a type already described | *Exemptions may be granted in exceptional cases. **Such** cases must be documented.* |

### 5. Comparative ellipsis
After *than* and *as*, repeated material is omitted: *Costs were higher in 2024 **than in 2023**.* *The northern route is as long as **the southern**.*

### Clarity first
Economy must never create ambiguity. *Raka visited Lina more often than his parents* could mean *than he visited his parents* or *than his parents visited her*. In such cases, add an auxiliary or a pronoun: *... than his parents **did*** or *... than he visited his parents*.

### Revision checklist
1. Is anything repeated that the reader could easily recover?
2. Are coordinated parts parallel in form?
3. Do lists linked by *respectively* match in number and order?
4. Could any reduced sentence be read in two ways?

sections.summary: Formal economy relies on gapping, conjunction reduction, respectively, likewise, do the same and such. All of them require parallel structures or matching lists, and none should create ambiguity; when in doubt, keep the auxiliary.

unitTestQuestions.explanation: Because the verb and object are identical, they can be omitted in the second clause, leaving only the contrasting elements: and Raka (got a distinction) in law.
